guide.title: Homecrest, Brooklyn: Homecrest-by-the-Sea and the Avenue U Strip
guide.intro: Homecrest began as an early-twentieth-century real estate subdivision. Developers put up large single-family homes in the east end of the town of Gravesend and marketed the district as Homecrest-by-the-Sea. The timing is legible in the transit record: the original at-grade station at Avenue U opened on the surface Brighton Beach Railroad near East 15th Street around 1902, described as coincident with the building of the community of Homecrest, and was replaced by the present elevated station around 1908. The neighborhood's boundaries have never settled — a 2010 walking tour placed it between about Kings Highway, Avenue X, Coney Island Avenue and Ocean Avenue, while other sources draw the lines differently — and the same tour noted that a few Victorian-style houses can still be found among the later blocks.

sections.heading: Old roads and small lanes
sections.body:
Kings Highway, which most descriptions put along Homecrest's northern side, has colonial roots. It was a Native American trail recorded as Mechawanienck in a 1652 deed, a wagon path in a 1682 deed, and was connected out of local roads and trails into a highway by the early eighteenth century, named for Kings County — which had itself been named for King Charles II in 1683. Gravesend Neck Road, which gives the Neck Road station its name, is described as a very old colonial-era road that predates the street grid, once running to a peninsula east of today's Nostrand Avenue called Gravesend Neck that landfill has since eliminated.

Neck Road station was also once a terminus of the Long Island Rail Road's Manhattan Beach Branch, with a separate spur branching off just south of it toward the now-razed Sheepshead Bay Race Track. No LIRR line serves Homecrest today.

Margaret Court is an easy-to-miss pedestrian walkway on East 13th Street between Avenues Y and Z, lined with small houses numbered 1 to 21; a 1929 Belcher Hyde atlas shows it already existed before the surrounding blocks were built out. Homecrest Court held one of the last remaining 1950s-era porcelain street signs in New York City when it was documented in 2013; that sign has since been removed and the lane carries no street sign now.

sections.heading: The Avenue U storefronts
sections.body:
Homecrest has long had a large Italian population, joined later by immigration from Latin America, China, Israel, Syria, Russia and South Asia. A Chinese enclave grew up right by the Avenue U subway station; the framing of it as Brooklyn's second Chinatown traces to bklynr rather than to Wikipedia, which describes the enclave without using that phrase.

The Avenue U storefronts on this page include Wing Hing Seafood Restaurant at 1217, Sheep by Barashka at 1223, Pho Vietnam Restaurant at 1243, Yuanzaibing at 1305, Long Wong Bakery at 1310, Karavan Grill at 1311 and Season Restaurant at 1321.

Where Homecrest gives way to Madison along Avenue U is not settled. The sources that describe Homecrest's edges disagree with one another and none should be treated as definitive, and the commercial strip carries on past these addresses into blocks commonly grouped with Madison.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The BMT Brighton Line runs through Homecrest, with stations at Kings Highway, Avenue U and Neck Road.

Kings Highway station, at Kings Highway between East 15th and East 16th Streets, sits on the border of Midwood and Homecrest. The Q stops there at all times and the B stops there on weekdays — rush hours, middays and early evenings — as an express.

Avenue U station, at Avenue U between East 15th and East 16th Streets, sits on the Homecrest and Sheepshead Bay border, served by the Q at all times.

Neck Road station, at Gravesend Neck Road between East 15th and East 16th Streets, is in Homecrest and is served by the Q at all times.

faq.question: How do I get to Homecrest?
faq.answer: By Q train, which stops at all times at Kings Highway, Avenue U and Neck Road on the BMT Brighton Line. Neck Road is in Homecrest; Kings Highway sits on the Midwood border and Avenue U on the Sheepshead Bay border. The B also stops at Kings Highway on weekdays during rush hours, middays and early evenings.

faq.question: Where are Homecrest's boundaries?
faq.answer: Sources disagree and none should be treated as settled. A 2010 walking-tour account places the neighborhood between about Kings Highway, Avenue X, Coney Island Avenue and Ocean Avenue; other accounts use Avenue V or Avenue U as the southern edge, East 16th Street or Ocean Parkway on the sides, and Avenue P on the north. The edge it shares with Madison along Avenue U is unsettled in the same way.

faq.question: Where does the name come from?
faq.answer: From Homecrest-by-the-Sea, the early-twentieth-century real estate development that put up large single-family homes in the east end of the town of Gravesend. A 2010 walking-tour account gives the same origin for the name.

faq.question: Where can I eat on Avenue U?
faq.answer: The addresses on this page run from 1217 to 1321: Wing Hing Seafood Restaurant, Sheep by Barashka, Pho Vietnam Restaurant, Yuanzaibing, Long Wong Bakery, Karavan Grill and Season Restaurant.

faq.question: Why are there two Kelly parks?
faq.answer: The city's parks-properties data carries two separate records under the name Kelly Park Playground in ZIP code 11229 — a 1.447-acre site at 1840 East 16 Street and a 3.449-acre site at 1301 Avenue S. NYC Parks' historical sign at the smaller one refers to a larger neighbor west of the BMT Brighton Beach transit line also named for William E. Kelly, and Wikipedia separately describes a William E. Kelly Memorial Park on Avenue S. Both records are listed here.

faq.question: Are there hotels in Homecrest?
faq.answer: No. A query of the city's property dataset for ZIP code 11229, Homecrest's primary ZIP, returned no property carrying a hotel building class. The neighboring guides linked from this page cover the surrounding area.

photos.title: Homecrest branch library, Coney Island Avenue
photos.description: The low glass-and-brick front of the Brooklyn Public Library's Homecrest branch, with book-return bins beside the door.
photos.author: QuasyBoy

photos.title: Homecrest Presbyterian Church
photos.description: A white clapboard church with a square louvered belfry under a cross finial, dormer windows along the roof and a lawn.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

photos.title: Tayba Islamic Center awning
photos.description: A green awning lettered Tayba Islamic Center over turquoise doors in a brick storefront row, fire escapes on the upper floors.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Brooklyn Public Library, Homecrest Branch
places.address: 2525 Coney Island Avenue at Avenue V, Brooklyn, NY 11223
places.summary: The neighborhood branch library on Coney Island Avenue, serving a large local immigrant population from Russia, China, Pakistan, India and Mexico.
places.history: It was used as a filming location for A Bronx Tale in 1993 and Brooklyn's Finest in 2009. The branch's address carries the 11223 ZIP code, a Gravesend-area code; its position on Coney Island Avenue, Homecrest's contested western edge, likely explains the mismatch.

photos.title: Homecrest branch library, Coney Island Avenue
photos.description: The low glass-and-brick front of the Brooklyn Public Library's Homecrest branch, with book-return bins beside the door.
photos.author: QuasyBoy

places.name: Kelly Park Playground
places.address: Avenue S at Moore Place, between East 16th and East 17th Streets, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: An NYC Parks playground with basketball courts, fitness equipment, a play area, spray showers and tennis courts. The city's parks-properties data records this site at 1840 East 16 Street, on 1.447 acres.
places.history: NYC Parks' historical sign names it for William E. Kelly, 1872 to 1929, a Brooklyn-born Kings County postmaster who later served as Clerk of Kings County until his death. The same sign refers to a larger neighbor west of the BMT Brighton Beach transit line also named for Kelly.

places.name: Kelly Park Playground, Avenue S
places.address: 1301 Avenue S, Brooklyn, NY 11229 (between East 14th and East 15th Streets)
places.summary: A 3.449-acre neighborhood park carried in the city's parks-properties data under the same name as the smaller Kelly Park Playground on East 16 Street, and in the same ZIP code.
places.history: This is the larger neighbor west of the BMT Brighton Beach transit line that NYC Parks' sign at the smaller playground refers to. Wikipedia describes a William E. Kelly Memorial Park on Avenue S between East 13th and East 14th Streets; the city's open data gives this property's cross streets as East 14th and East 15th, one block apart from that description.

places.name: Mellett Playground
places.address: 1301 Avenue V, Brooklyn, NY 11229 (between East 13th and East 14th Streets)
places.summary: A neighborhood park with basketball and handball courts, a playground, public restrooms, soccer fields and spray showers.
places.history: Named for Corporal Francis J. and Private John Mellett, brothers from the Sheepshead Bay area who died serving in the Second World War.

places.name: Homecrest Playground
places.address: Belt Parkway and Williams Court, between East 12th Street and Homecrest Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11235
places.summary: A playground founded in 1940, with basketball and handball courts, a play area, soccer fields and spray showers. NYC Parks records it in ZIP code 11235, a Sheepshead Bay-area code, so it sits near Homecrest's southern edge and its neighborhood affiliation is approximate.

places.name: Wing Hing Seafood Restaurant
places.summary: A Chinese seafood restaurant with a wall of tanks near the entrance for choosing live seafood. The menu runs to ginger scallion lobster and crab, clams with black bean sauce, razor clams, and a bone-in Peking-style pork chop fried crisp with sweet and sour sauce. Full dim sum service runs at weekends, with a smaller to-go selection during the week.

places.name: Sheep by Barashka
places.summary: A restaurant serving lunch, dinner, banquets and delivery, with live music, and listed on a venue-rental marketplace as bookable for private dining and parties. Its own description of the food is 'authentic cuisine with modern flair.' Open Wednesday to Friday noon to 10pm and Saturday and Sunday noon to 11pm.

places.name: Pho Vietnam Restaurant
places.summary: A Vietnamese restaurant, which trades on its own site as Pho Viet Nam. Its bowls include an Extra Big Bowl Combination (Xe Lua), a Special Big Bowl with Beef Ball Combination, a Small Rice Noodle Soup Combination and a crab, pork and tomato vermicelli noodle soup. Closed Monday; Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30am to 9pm.

places.name: Yuanzaibing
places.summary: A restaurant whose name is rendered in Chinese as 汶村圓仔炳 五味鵝. The last three characters translate as 'five spice goose,' indicating a specialty dish.

places.name: Long Wong Bakery
places.history: A separate write-up of the avenue's Chinese businesses names a Long Wong Bakery II without giving an address.

places.name: Karavan Grill
places.summary: A halal restaurant serving Middle Eastern and Mediterranean food with Tajik and Russian influences, Qurutob and Plov among the dishes, with live music on selected nights. It states that it holds to 'strict Halal standards in every part of our kitchen,' and its operating entity is Karavan Kebab LLC, the name it carries on some listings. Its own site gives hours of 11am to 11pm daily; a second listing for the same address posts different hours.

places.name: Season Restaurant
places.summary: A Cantonese restaurant, known in Chinese as 三喜酒家, serving dim sum daily alongside roasted meats; reviewers single out a crispy roasted pork. It carries a large tea selection.

entries.name: Brooklyn Public Library, Homecrest Branch
entries.note: The Coney Island Avenue branch, seen on screen in A Bronx Tale and Brooklyn's Finest.

entries.name: Kelly Park Playground
entries.note: Courts and tennis off Avenue S, named for a Kings County postmaster and county clerk.

entries.name: Kelly Park Playground, Avenue S
entries.note: The larger of the two Kelly records, 3.449 acres at 1301 Avenue S.

entries.name: Mellett Playground
entries.note: Courts, soccer fields and spray showers on Avenue V, named for two brothers who died in the Second World War.

entries.name: Homecrest Playground
entries.note: Ballfields and courts by the Belt Parkway, founded in 1940.

entries.name: Wing Hing Seafood Restaurant
entries.note: A Chinese seafood restaurant at 1217 Avenue U, with tanks of live seafood by the entrance and full dim sum at weekends.

entries.name: Sheep by Barashka
entries.note: A restaurant at 1223 Avenue U with live music, open Wednesday to Sunday from noon.

entries.name: Pho Vietnam Restaurant
entries.note: A Vietnamese restaurant at 1243 Avenue U, trading on its own site as Pho Viet Nam. Closed Mondays.

entries.name: Yuanzaibing
entries.note: A restaurant at 1305 Avenue U whose Chinese name ends in 五味鵝, 'five spice goose.'

entries.name: Long Wong Bakery
entries.note: A bakery at 1310 Avenue U, on the strip Wikipedia describes as a Chinese enclave by the subway station.

entries.name: Karavan Grill
entries.note: A halal Middle Eastern and Mediterranean kitchen at 1311 Avenue U, also listed as Karavan Kebab.

entries.name: Season Restaurant
entries.note: A Cantonese restaurant at 1321 Avenue U, with dim sum daily and roasted meats.

links.note: Homecrest began as Homecrest-by-the-Sea, a development of large single-family homes in the east end of the town of Gravesend.
Avenue U station sits on the Homecrest and Sheepshead Bay border, and Neck Road station is in Homecrest immediately adjacent to Sheepshead Bay.
Kings Highway station, at Kings Highway between East 15th and East 16th Streets, sits on the border of Midwood and Homecrest.
